newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Housing starts, jobless claims.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Housing starts, jobless claims.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market gets August housing starts data, the weekly report on new jobless claims and the Philalphia Fed index on Thursday.
Barring a surprisingly sharp move in jobless claims, the housing data likely will interest the market most.

"The report that's most important is the housing starts," said Dana Johnson, head of research for First Chicago Capital Markets. "Housing is a key rate-sensitive sector of the economy and the degree to which it is being affected by higher interest rates bears on how rapidly the economy is likely to slow."
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that housing starts slowed moderately in August to an annualized rate of 1.445 million units from 1.46 million units in July.
"Starts are starting to level off," said Johnson. "If they were surprisingly strongly strong or weak, that would affect the comfort level of the market."

"Housing is interesting because the National Association of Home Builders' buyers traffic index dropped pretty sharply in September," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

"It suggests that 8-1/4 percent mortgage yields are finally starting to have a negative impact on housing so there is a potential for a surprise there," said Rupkey. "There might be a weaker number than people anticipate."

New claims for state unemployment insurance, meanwhile, have "pretty clearly settled into a lower range than they had been in June and July, suggesting that the labor market is pretty reactive, pretty strong," said Johnson.
Economists Reuters surveyed estimated, on average, that jobless claims edged a bit lower in the week ended September 14 -- to 335,000 from 338,000 a week earlier.
"If claims rose substantially, I'd be more accepting of the story that economic growth is slowing," said Johnson.
"It's pretty important to keep your eye on the four-week moving average for jobless claims," Johnson said. The four-week moving average was 327,750, as of the week ended September 7.
"In June and July, the four-week moving average for new jobless claims was 350,000 to 360,000 and it's moved down rather sharply to the 320,000 to 330,000 range," said Johnson.
"If it stays there, that would seem to imply to me that labor markets are remaining pretty strong," he said.
"Claims got credit last week as being a factor that helped the market to rally, but it's still expected to reflect a huge improvement in the labor markets," agreed Rupkey.

"If you go back to the June payroll period, the average weekly claims were 357,000. In the July period, they were 367,000," said Rupkey. "So even though last week was 338,000, that's still a vast improvement.
"I would think the jobless claims data would only hurt the market," said Rupkey. "It's a potential negative."
Investors will also look at the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's September index of local business conditions.
Housing starts and jobless claims data are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. The Philadephia Fed index is due at 1000 EDT.

"Given the strength in industrial production in August, maybe this September Philly Fed number could move up to something like 25 (from 21.5 in August)," Rupkey said. "That could be a small problem for the market."

But Rupkey said, "realistically, we're probably just going to move a little off technicals here." After the market's recent retreat, "it might be time to come up in the other direction once we wade through all this data," he said.
Dealers indicated Fed funds would open near 5-1/8 percent on Thursday. -- 212-859-1679
